Abstract

The rapid proliferation of commercial Internet of Things (IoT) appliances has drastically expanded the cyberattack surface, exposing vulnerable smart home devices to large-scale distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) botnets such as Mirai and BASHLITE (Gafgyt). While deep neural networks provide strong anomaly detection capabilities, their substantial memory footprint, matrix multiplication overhead, and black-box nature severely limit real-time inline deployment on resource-constrained IoT gateways and edge microcontrollers. In this work, as part of the Group 1 research framework inspired by "Lightweight Android and IoT Botnet Detection Using C4.5 Decision Trees", we design, audit, and benchmark a regularized Classification and Regression Tree (CART) architecture trained on the benchmark N-BaIoT dataset (7,062,606 network flow records across 89 packet captures from 9 commercial IoT devices). To eliminate test-set selection bias, we introduce a strict 3-way Train / Validation / Test separation protocol: effective minimal cost-complexity pruning parameters (α) were generated exclusively on an internal training subset (N=82,153) and swept across an internal validation set (N=20,539). The selected optimal parameter α* = 1.9998 × 10-5 was retrained on the full training partition (N=102,692) and evaluated exactly once on the held-out test partition (N=25,674). Pruning reduced maximum tree depth from 21 to 18 levels (-14.3%), node count from 181 to 133 (-26.5%), terminal leaves from 91 to 67 (-26.4%), and closed the train-test generalization overfitting gap from 0.1022% to 0.0769%, while preserving peak multiclass test accuracy of 99.6183%, macro F1-score of 99.6510%, and near-perfect binary attack detection accuracy of 99.9649% (F1: 99.9810%). Hardware latency benchmarking on an ARM64 testbed demonstrates a per-packet sequential latency of 34.41 μs (29,062 pkts/s) and a batch amortized throughput of 12,036,209 pkts/s, with a compact serialized model size of only 5.44 KB, verifying edge feasibility.

1. Introduction & Research Motivation

The ecosystem of Internet of Things (IoT) hardware—ranging from IP video doorbells and smart baby monitors to security webcams and digital signage—is characterized by constrained processing power, minimal local RAM (frequently under 256 KB to 16 MB), and often neglected firmware security patching. Consequently, IoT devices represent ideal targets for malicious actors seeking to assemble massive botnet armies. The Mirai and BASHLITE (Gafgyt) malware families continuously scan IP subnets for exposed telnet/SSH services and vulnerable IoT daemon ports, propagate automated brute-force attacks, install malicious executables, and coordinate destructive flood campaigns (SYN, ACK, UDP, and UDP-plain attacks).

To mitigate these threats, intrusion detection systems (IDS) must operate directly at the local IoT network gateway or on edge routing appliances. However, conventional deep learning models—such as the autoencoders proposed in the N-BaIoT base paper—incur non-trivial floating-point matrix multiplication costs and floating-point reconstruction latency. Decision Trees present a compelling alternative: inference reduces to a deterministic sequence of scalar threshold comparisons (I(Xj ≤ θ)), executing in O(h) time where h is the tree depth. Furthermore, every decision path is fully transparent and auditable, enabling direct translation into router firewall rules or C-based microcontroller code.

2. Related Work & Theoretical Grounding

Our experimental framework is grounded in three foundational literature pillars:

  • Base Paper — Meidan et al. (2018): In "N-BaIoT: Network-based Detection of IoT Botnet Attacks Using Deep Autoencoders" (IEEE Pervasive Computing), Meidan et al. introduced the N-BaIoT benchmark by capturing raw traffic from 9 commercial IoT devices infected with Mirai and Gafgyt. They extracted 115 continuous statistical features using the Kitsune damped window engine and trained 9 device-specific deep autoencoders on benign traffic. An anomaly was flagged when reconstruction error (MSE) exceeded a threshold. While effective, separate autoencoders for every device require substantial memory and matrix algebra.
  • Shafiq et al. (2021): In "CORRAUC: A Malicious Bot-IoT Traffic Detection Method in IoT Network Using Machine-Learning Techniques" (IEEE Internet of Things Journal), the authors developed a correlation-AUC feature selection framework across IoT botnet traffic, demonstrating that compact decision trees achieve near-identical detection rates to complex ensembles when fed salient flow features.
  • Moubayed et al. (2020): In "Optimized Machine Learning-Based Network Intrusion Detection for IoT Networks" (IEEE Internet of Things Journal), the authors analyzed tree regularization, establishing that cost-complexity pruning eliminates over-specialized leaf nodes, reduces tree complexity by over 40%, and accelerates inference without compromising F1-score.

Methodological Distinction: CART vs. C4.5

The assigned Group 1 research framework references the C4.5 Decision Tree paradigm (Quinlan, 1993). In our Python implementation, we utilize sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier, which implements an optimized version of Breiman's CART algorithm (Breiman et al., 1984). The core mathematical distinctions are formalized below:

Architectural Dimension C4.5 Paradigm (Quinlan, 1993) CART Implementation (Breiman et al., 1984 / scikit-learn)
Splitting Topology Multiway splits on nominal categorical attributes; binary on continuous Strictly binary recursive splitting (≤ θ vs. > θ) across all features
Splitting Criterion Information Gain Ratio: GainRatio(S, A) = Gain(S, A) / SplitInfo(S, A) Gini Impurity Reduction: ΔIG(t) = IG(t) - (NL/Nt)IG(tL) - (NR/Nt)IG(tR)
Pruning Strategy Pessimistic Error Pruning (PEP) using binomial confidence intervals Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning parameterized by α ≥ 0 (ccp_α)
Continuous Features Sorts continuous values and tests candidate binary thresholds Identical: sorts continuous attributes and evaluates midpoint binary splits

Because the N-BaIoT dataset consists exclusively of continuous numerical features, CART's binary thresholding evaluates the exact same decision surface as continuous C4.5 splits, while minimal cost-complexity pruning provides a mathematically principled regularization parameter α.

3. Dataset Architecture, Feature Engineering & Sampling Integrity

The raw N-BaIoT dataset (verified intact in /archive) contains 7,062,606 packet records distributed across 89 CSV files and 9 commercial IoT devices. Each record comprises 115 continuous flow features generated by Kitsune's damped sliding window algorithm across 5 decay windows: λ ∈ {100ms, 500ms, 1.5s, 10s, 1min}.

Port / Socket Terminology Clarification

A common misconception in N-BaIoT analysis is to interpret stream labels as literal integer port numbers. N-BaIoT does not contain raw packet header fields such as source/destination IP strings, TCP/UDP port numbers (e.g., 80, 443), or protocol flag bits. Instead:

  • H captures outbound statistics from the source host.
  • HH captures host-to-host conversational statistics (e.g., jitter, packet size).
  • HpHp captures Host+Port-to-Host+Port socket-stream statistical aggregates. The sub-identifier L1 denotes decay factor λ=1. Thus, HpHp_L1_weight represents the socket packet arrival weight at decay λ=1, not port number 1.

Deterministic Systematic Sampling & Verification

To respect the 16.0 GB host RAM constraint while preserving temporal structure across all 89 files, we applied deterministic systematic row-step sampling with a fixed stride step=55, extracting an experimental corpus of 128,366 samples (56.4 MB in RAM).

Data Leakage Audit

The preprocessing pipeline was audited to ensure strict zero-leakage isolation:

  • Target Leakage: Labels (label_11, label_bin) and metadata (device_id) were stripped prior to model fitting.
  • Identity Leakage: No source/destination IPs, MAC addresses, or packet timestamps exist in the feature set.
  • Contamination: Decision trees are scale-invariant; no global transformers or scalers were fitted across splits.
  • Partition Disjointness: Train (N=102,692) and Test (N=25,674) index sets share zero intersection (Overlap = 0).

4. Machine Learning Formulation & Pruning Strategy

For node t with class probabilities p(c|t), Gini Impurity is defined as:

IG(t) = 1 - ∑ p(c|t)2 = ∑i ≠ j p(i|t) p(j|t)

CART selects feature j* and split threshold θ* to maximize the impurity decrease ΔIG(t). Unconstrained greedy splitting results in deep trees that memorize transient packet fluctuations.

Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning (ccp_α) Formulation

To regularize tree complexity, we employ Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning (Breiman et al., 1984). For any subtree T ⊆ Tmax, the cost-complexity criterion is parameterized by α ≥ 0:

Rα(T) = R(T) + α |T|

where R(T) is total leaf impurity/misclassification rate, |T| is the number of terminal leaves, and α is the complexity penalty per additional leaf split. For each internal node t, the effective alpha where collapsing the subtree Tt into node t yields equal cost is:

αeff(t) = (R(t) - R(Tt)) / (|Tt| - 1)

Validation-Isolated Pruning Protocol

To prevent test-set selection bias, the full training partition (N=102,692) was internally split into an Internal Training Subset (N=82,153) and an Internal Validation Set (N=20,539). The pruning path was extracted strictly from the internal training subset, yielding 60 candidate α thresholds. 20 representative candidates were evaluated exclusively on the validation set.

Fig. 2. Validation Macro F1 vs. Cost-Complexity Alpha (α).
Fig. 3. Terminal Leaf Count (|T|) vs. Pruning Parameter α.

Optimal Selection: Candidate ID 2 with α* = 1.999753 × 10-5 ≈ 1.9998 × 10-5 achieved the highest validation macro F1-score (99.7696%) and validation accuracy (99.7127%) while reducing leaf splits to 65 on the validation tree.

Hardware & Edge Complexity Analysis

  • Time Complexity: At runtime, each packet traverses from root to leaf in at most h=18 scalar comparisons, requiring O(h) operations with zero floating-point matrix arithmetic.
  • Sequential Latency: Single-sample inspection takes 34.41 μs (29,062 packets/s), which includes Python interpreter dispatch and array wrapping. In compiled C/firmware, this reduces to sub-microsecond scalar branching.
  • Batch Throughput: Under buffered bulk inspection (N=25,674), amortized traversal requires only 0.083 μs per packet, achieving 12.04 million packets/second.
  • Flash Footprint: The complete serialized model occupies only 5.44 KB on disk (and < 100 KB in RAM), easily fitting inside L1/L2 CPU caches or standard microcontroller flash (e.g., STM32, ESP32).

9. Conclusion & Remaining Manual Tasks

This investigation demonstrates that regularized CART Decision Trees—when trained with a validation-isolated minimal cost-complexity pruning protocol—provide an exceptionally lightweight, transparent, and accurate solution for IoT botnet attack detection on the N-BaIoT benchmark. The final pruned tree achieves 99.62% multiclass test accuracy and 99.96% binary detection accuracy while reducing structural node count by 26.5% and maintaining a microsecond-scale execution profile with a 5.44 KB model footprint.
